what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: News should sell the evidence, not the article
sections.para: Advertising and subscriptions both fail the reader, and falling search traffic and consumer law arriving in January 2027 are dismantling them. The proposal is to treat the story as a fractal semantic graph, with the article as one projection, and sell five things from it in pence to readers, firms and agents, paying whoever made the facts.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Sell five projections of one evidenced story graph
sections.para: The whole argument in ten points: both models fail readers and are being dismantled, the goal is a loop that funds investigative work, and the article is one projection of a fractal graph. Five things can be sold, revenue would split 60/25/10/5 towards the researcher, and parts already run, though the billing does not.

sections.label: Both models are bad for the reader
sections.line: Advertising sells the reader; subscriptions charge rent on disuse
sections.para: Under advertising the reader is inventory and content is bait; under subscriptions the reader pays 100% for the 10% they use, as in one household paying roughly £50 a month. Neither funds reliability, so investigative work is cut first. Reuters Institute 2026 data puts trust in news at 37% and news avoidance at 42%.

sections.label: The objective, stated once
sections.line: The goal is a model that rewards investigative journalism
sections.para: Not a better paywall or a cheaper subscription, but a loop: evidenced reporting drives on-demand use by readers, firms and agents, that use produces revenue independent of search traffic and subscriber inertia, and the revenue funds more reporting. A proposal that does not reward the reporting is not part of the model, however well it monetises.

sections.label: The two clocks, briefly
sections.line: Search traffic and subscription inertia are both being removed
sections.para: Organic Google traffic to publishers fell 33% globally in the year to November 2025, and Cloudflare now tolls AI crawlers with HTTP 402. Only 17% pay for online news, and UK subscription rules, brought forward to 1 January 2027, remove the inertia subscriptions depend on. The industry still answers with more subscriptions and personalisation.

sections.label: Why paying per item failed before, and why that is about the wrong thing
sections.line: Micropayment critiques assume a reader; today's buyers differ
sections.para: James Ball's 2020 case and Blendle's record, 150,000 payers among more than a million users, show readers will not weigh twenty pence per article. But the buyers have changed: the reader wants one item, the firm wants a licence to transform and forward it, and the agent pays per query to learn whether it is true.

sections.label: The story is a graph, and the article is a projection
sections.line: The story is a graph; articles are projections
sections.para: A story is claims, evidence, sources, raw materials and drafts; the article is one walk through it, and the industry sells that cheapest projection while the graph decays. The dataset is worth more than the words, which any model can regenerate. I have argued this since February 2025, before the evidence arrived to confirm it.

sections.label: The graph is fractal, and meaning comes from connectivity
sections.line: Meaning lives in edges, and every node opens further
sections.para: In a Fractal Semantic Graph every edge is a verb with a named inverse, such as evidenced_by or contradicts, which is how reporters already connect facts. Zooming into any node opens its own world. This gives provenance down to the byte, corrections that propagate, projections sized to the question, and credit for doors that turned out empty.

sections.label: Trust through provenance, provenance via evidence
sections.line: Evidence is hashed bytes, provenance the path, trust earned
sections.para: Evidence is frozen, SHA-256 hashed bytes rather than links. Provenance is the path of named edges from a claim down to that evidence, a checkable statement of what it rests on rather than of truth. Trust is earned when walked provenance keeps holding. Each step can be sold, and the article alone contains none of them.

sections.label: What a story vault holds
sections.line: A vault holds the whole story as one unit
sections.para: An encrypted, versioned vault holds the text, evidence, story graph, sources, translations and prompts. Sources are frozen and hashed, claims are superseded rather than deleted, anonymous sources are flagged for automatic redaction, and credibility is computed from consistency. A worked example cost £8.40 and six hours twenty-three minutes of compute, with zero human hours.

sections.label: Five things to sell, and how each one works
sections.line: One graph yields five products, with the article free
sections.para: The public article stays free and findable as the door. The licensed article sells in pence to readers and as a licence to transform for firms. The evidence vault serves analysts and lawyers, customised projections cut the graph per role or language, and the verification API sells warranted, on-record confirmation per query.

sections.label: Who gets paid, and how the money moves
sections.line: Payments should flow mostly to whoever made the fact
sections.para: The proposed split is 60% to the original researcher, 25% to the data organisation, 10% to the journalist and 5% to the outlet, which today captures nearly everything. Paying sources requires a graph that names them. Rails such as x402 now make payments in pence viable, though nothing on sgit.ai is wired to them yet.

sections.label: The parts that already run
sections.line: The substrate already runs in public, cheaply
sections.para: Working pieces include the hash-verified Regulation Graph, VoiceDebrief, a penetration test report with eight audience views, and the Portuguese newsroom with 92 frozen sources, 312 nodes and 942 edges behind an editor-gated pipeline. The whole estate of thirty-one vaults is 2,662 files and 295 MB, so even one journalist could run it.

sections.label: What I would do, if I ran a publisher
sections.line: Eight steps a publisher could start this quarter
sections.para: Store stories as graphs from day one and freeze and hash every source. Keep the public article free and findable, sell licensed articles in pence, and adopt the five subscription clauses before January. License the evidence vault to B2B buyers, put corrections in the graph, and publish the cost per story.

sections.label: The dataset was always worth more than the article
sections.line: The graph, not the words, is what buyers miss
sections.para: The industry sells the output whose marginal cost has gone to zero and discards the asset that has not. The evidence, trail, on-record confirmation and tailored view, paid in pence to those who made the facts, is the product. Take away the words and few notice; take away the graph and lawyers, analysts and agents do.
